newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals - Zinc seen rallying to $1,600/tonne.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Zinc seen rallying to $1,600/tonne.

text.p: The latest rally in zinc to a seven-year peak on the London Metal Exchange (LME) is likely to continue until prices hit the psychologically key level of $1,600 per tonne, Asian traders said on Wednesday.
"It will certainly reach the $1,600 level. I can't wait to see what happens then," said a zinc trader at one of Japan's major trading houses.
Traders here agreed that benchmark three-month zinc was now eyeing the $1,600 level after achieving $1,545, its highest since August 1990, in London on Tuesday.
"Once it breaches the $1,550 level, the advance will gain momentum from fund buying," said a trader at a European house. "After reaching $1,600, a correction may be in store," he said.
Traders said Japan's physical zinc market remained tight as many users had digested a large portion of their imports in April under a special once-a-year tariff exemption scheme.
"We're bringing in quite a lot of Chinese metal directly from Chinese and Singaporean warehouses," said another trader.
He said the Japanese market was likely to remain tight until the end of September and that domestic demand hinges on Japanese car exports.
"If that (car exports) collapses, the situation could deteriorate quite quickly as demand from the construction sector is not that good," the trader added.

Japanese premiums for zinc, despite firm demand, remained low at $20-$30 per tonne over LME cah prices, reflecting aggressive exports from China. Traders said some Chinese sources were offering zinc at par with LME prices.

In the aluminium market, traders were surprised that three-month metal on the LME climbed to $1,615 a tonne, well above the key $1,600 level, as they had believed the upside was heavy despite relatively healthy fundamentals.

"It looks set to move upwards towards $1,650," said one trader, who added that the U.S. economy did not look bad in spite of remarks by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Tuesday that the country's economic growth was slowing.
Physical aluminium trade in Japan ground to a halt due to the rise on the LME and the country's high premiums, which remained at $95-$100 per tonne for spot deliveries this quarter.
Premiums for the fourth quarter were slightly lower at around $90 per tonne, amid expectations that domestic demand may start showing signs of weakness, traders said.
"It's clear that demand from the construction and car industries is declining, but it remains unclear how the market will look after the summer holidays," said one trader.
Japan's physical copper market also remained quiet with players watching whether the LME's cash/threes backwardation would narrow further to less than $100 a tonne after hitting $270 last week.
Copper premiums were unchanged at $50-$60 per tonne, although hardly any spot deals have been done recently, particularly as end-users have large stocks, traders said.
"I don't expect any demand for a while," said one trader. "It depends on the weather during the summer, but I'm not too optimistic on demand for air conditioners."
